title: A high-stakes last day at the Olympics. Plus: 1 more figure skating show
content:
Games Briefing 🏅 | This is The Athletic’s daily newsletter for the Milan Cortina Olympics. Sign up here to receive the Games Briefing directly in your inbox.

MILAN — Just a handful of golds left to hand out! What’s left on your list to watch? Here’s what we’re looking at:

🔥 Men’s hockey showdown
🇳🇴 Klæbo’s dominance
📈 Women’s hockey viewership

To stay on top of everything this weekend, stick with our ongoing live coverage.

We’d also love to hear from you about your most memorable moments from these Olympics! If you’d like to participate, please fill out this survey, and with your permission, we’ll include some responses in a future newsletter.

Yes, it’s a fun matchup — the United States and Canada men’s hockey teams, packed with many of the top NHL stars, going head to head for Olympic gold and a clear upper hand in a captivating rivalry.

Yet the marquee competition Sunday, the last day of these Winter Olympics, is perhaps even more consequential than that, our senior hockey columnist Pierre LeBrun believes. It could end up as the most-watched game in the history of the sport.

“That’s exciting for everybody involved, players, countries, all the people back home, it’s going to be a really special moment, just to have an opportunity to achieve your childhood dream, nothing better than that,’’ said Team USA star forward Brady Tkachuk.

A big part of the excitement is that on the ice, in this Olympic format with a three-on-three overtime, this feels like a legitimate coin-flip matchup. Some context:

Fitting that it’ll be the last gold medal of these Olympics. Watch it at 8:10 a.m. ET on NBC and Peacock.

🤯 Johannes Høsflot Klæbo of Norway, one of the unquestioned stars of these Olympics, grabbed his sixth gold in six events, running up his record Winter Games total to 11 golds. He talked with Jacob Whitehead about his pursuit of dominance. “I’m just chasing the feeling of those last 100 meters,” he said. “That’s what I do this all for.”

✏️ The New York Times also looked at how Klæbo’s performances have compared with all-time great Olympians.

📺 Speaking of popular hockey games, Thursday’s U.S.-Canada women’s final was the most-watched women’s hockey game on record.

🥌 It’s 🇨🇦> 🇺🇸 for women’s curling bronze.

🏁 American Jordan Stolz ends these Olympics with three speedskating medals, including two golds and a silver, yet fell just shy of the podium with a fourth-place finish in mass start.

🪩 Figure skating is putting on one more show — not for any medals, but just for fun. Americans Alysa Liu, Ilia Malinin, Amber Glenn and many others are performing in an exhibition gala shortly, a tradition to close out the sport each Olympics. We’ll be here watching at 2 p.m. ET.

🏠 For the NHLers, living in the Olympic athletes’ village has made for some weird encounters.

📍 There’s a trading center for pins here, and it’s taking a traditional spectator pastime and ramping it way up.

One of the things that is hard to convey on television is the extent to which volunteers — more than 18,000 of them! — are at the heart of the Olympics. Lindsay Schnell, in this video, explains their presence in the various clusters across Italy:

The two biggest moments Sunday are the U.S-Canada men’s hockey gold medal game, followed by the closing ceremony (2:30 p.m. ET) from Verona, Italy. There will be four other gold medals awarded:

The cross-country race will be the last of American star Jessie Diggins’ Olympic career. The New York Times Magazine has more on how she tested the limits of endurance to get here.

And the freestyle skiing final was postponed from Saturday, meaning that Sunday will feature Eileen Gu’s last event.

Here’s a look at the medal race with 109 events down and seven remaining. Norway has broken its own record for the most medals at one Winter Games:
